transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

My mind just won’t shut off about work and everything else, and I can’t seem to turn the worrying off no matter what I do. It’s just gotten to a point where I feel completely overwhelmed, and a friend suggested I should finally talk to someone.

Have you been having sudden episodes of intense fear or physical symptoms like a racing heart, shortness of breath, chest tightness, dizziness, or feeling like you might lose control that peak within minutes? Or is it more of a constant worry that stays with you most days?

It’s definitely more of a constant, ongoing worry rather than sudden panic attacks. My mind is just constantly running worst-case scenarios, and I feel wired and tense almost all the time. It doesn't really peak and go away; it's just always there in the background.
How long have you been feeling this constant worry and tension most days? Did it start after a specific stressful event, or has it been going on for 6 months or longer?

It’s been going on for about nine months now. It started right around the time I got promoted at work and took on a lot of new, complex responsibilities. I became the primary bilingual contact for a major corporate client, and the pressure has just been building since then.

If your work situation improved or the promotion-related pressure went away, do you think the worry would mostly disappear, or do you tend to worry excessively about many areas of life even apart from that stress? Has this kind of broad, hard-to-control worrying happened to you before this job change?

Even if work got better, I don't think the worrying would just disappear because it has spread to other things, like my parents' health and my student loans. I've never experienced this kind of broad, uncontrollable worry before the promotion; it really only started being this overwhelming about nine months ago.

Since this started after your promotion, do the worry and tension still feel mostly tied to that work stress, or do they now seem excessive and hard to control even when you’re not thinking about the promotion? Have these symptoms continued even during times when work pressure briefly eased up?

It doesn't feel tied only to work anymore, as the worrying has expanded to things like my parents' health and my student loans even when work is quiet. Once it starts, it's like a YouTube autoplay I can't pause, and I can't shut it off even when I'm exhausted and trying to relax. It just feels completely uncontrollable no matter what is going on.

Before the promotion, were you generally a worrier, or did this pattern of excessive worry begin only after that stress and stay closely linked to it? In other words, does it feel like a reaction to that life change, or more like a new ongoing anxiety problem of its own?

Before the promotion, I was actually pretty good at staying grounded and keeping a healthy balance, so I wasn't really a chronic worrier. Now, it definitely feels like a new, ongoing anxiety problem of its own. The worrying has spiraled way beyond work to things like my parents' health and my student loans, and I just can't seem to shut it off anymore.

Along with the worry, have you been having symptoms like trouble sleeping, feeling restless or on edge, muscle tension, irritability, trouble concentrating, or getting tired easily? How much are these symptoms affecting your daily life at work, at home, or socially?

Yes, I'm dealing with almost all of those—I feel constantly wired and clench my shoulders, my mind goes blank during calls, and I'm often staring at the ceiling at 2 a.m. only to wake up completely unrefreshed. It’s really impacting my life because I've started missing project deadlines, zoning out in client meetings, and canceling plans with friends or skipping my dance nights because I'm just too drained.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports excessive, difficult-to-control worry occurring most days for about 9 months, generalized across multiple domains beyond the original work stressor, with associated restlessness, muscle tension, insomnia, poor concentration, fatigue, and significant occupational/social impairment. Although symptoms began after a promotion, they have evolved beyond a circumscribed stress reaction, making generalized anxiety disorder more consistent than adjustment disorder.
